articles.title: I wish tech companies knew more about me
articles.summary:
"Tech companies are spying on us" is a truism at this point. Endless articles and investigations have ensured that everybody is aware: they are spying on us, they listen to our conversations, they know more about us than we know ourselves, they know you're going to be fired or become pregnant or become depressed before it happens...
I have never felt anything close to that.
I get shown ads for products I just purchased. All this spying, machine learning, big data result in "he bought a mattress, show him more mattresses". Here, I literally just opened a random website with no adblocker, and I see a purple gamepad I recently purchased, with two other gamepads:

When listening to personalized playlists on Spotify and YouTube Music I skip every single electronic track with vocals. I listen to a lot of techno and related genres, and the moment someone starts singing I skip the track. I've been doing it for years. None of these advanced algorithms have ever noticed this simple pattern.
Using Google Chrome, logged into my Google account, I searched for info about Google AI plan usage limits, got an AI-generated response with a link to the help page, clicked it and ended up, logged out, on a Finnish-language landing page (because I'm located in Finland).

My user account, system locale, browser locale, and keyboard settings are all set to English. I am logged into Chrome and all Google services. 
I travel to Germany every few months, and lots of services that I've been using for years suddenly decide I speak German. 
The PlayStation online store is in Finnish, while some menus are in English, and even if I switch the website language to English (via a hidden, clunky selector), it resets back after a few clicks or after opening a new tab. 

Here's an ad for some smart home wellness system. I click on it: they don't deliver to Finland. 

A full page of repeating ads for industrial-grade light-curing, methacrylate-based resin designed for 3D printing. I don't have a 3D printer and have no idea what this is.

I clicked on that ad; now I keep getting other 3D-printing-related ads. 

Here's an ad for an email/WhatsApp marketing tool. I never needed any marketing tool, nor do I own a WhatsApp business account.

Now it's a Helsinki hotel. I live in Helsinki, I haven't searched for local hotels since 2014 when I first arrived here.

A fucking asphalt cleaning tractor.

I searched YouTube for installation instruction for a specific appliance "AEG CCS84751", watched a couple of relevant videos and the next day saw my homepage populated with more videos about random ovens and stoves. OK, so, let's see, a user searches for installation instructions for a very specific, concrete model. What could we machine-learn from this, what are the options here?
The user is into ovens
The user is into installing appliances
The user needs this one particular instruction for this one particular oven because the user maybe bought that oven and wants to install it, once, maybe?
My bank keeps sending me offers for car insurance. I have car insurance with that bank. Have had it for years.
An airline, when reminding me of an upcoming trip, send info about visas and border crossing laws which don't apply to my citizenship. They literally have a scan of my passport.
Netflix on Apple TV asks me to select a user every time I launch it. I've  had this account for 15+ years, and never had more than one user on it. I always select the only option there is to select. There is no setting to disable this screen.
My mobile provider keeps sending me discounts for children's products and events from their corporate partners. I don't have children.
HBO keeps recommending me foreign movies and shows which I cannot watch as they don't have English subtitles.
I have no doubts that a lot of information is being tracked, stored, and sold. Since that's already done, could you guys at least use some of it?..

articles.title: Chance Miller Reviews the New A20 Pro iPad Mini
articles.summary:
Chance Miller, writing at 9to5Mac:
Unfortunately, the new iPad mini’s screen has one limitation: it
doesn’t support ProMotion, or a 120Hz refresh rate of any kind.
Instead, it’s still locked to 60Hz. This is an incredibly
frustrating decision that I can’t quite wrap my head around.
Apple touts the iPad mini’s OLED screen as offering
significantly faster pixel response time than the previous
generation’s LCD panel, leading to improvements like smoother
scrolling and reduced motion blur.
I’ve noticed that things like swiping between Home Screen pages,
scrolling social media, and system animations are noticeably
smoother. They aren’t, however, as smooth as an Apple device with
a ProMotion display, and they’re not a substitute for a higher
refresh-rate display.
Apple is very stingy with ProMotion. Until last year it was exclusively available in iPhones, iPads, and MacBooks that had “Pro” in their name. Last year they added ProMotion to two products without “Pro” in their names: the iPhone 17 and iPhone Air. This year’s $2,000 iPhone Duo of course offers it now too. Apple refreshed the $1,600 Studio Display last year but it still only supports 60 Hz; only the $3,300 Studio Display XDR supports 120 Hz. (Apple does not call this “ProMotion”.)
What makes this frustrating with the iPad Mini is that Apple doesn’t sell an iPad Pro smaller than 11 inches. With MacBooks and larger iPads, if you really care about ProMotion, you can spend money to get it. With a small iPad, however, you can’t.
My big question re: the new iPad Mini is the new “acoustic display”. Miller gives it a thumbs-up:
Essentially, Apple has designed special woofers that vibrate the
display to produce low and midrange frequencies. For higher
frequencies, custom tweeters are hidden between the glass and
aluminum enclosure. Apple says this new system delivers louder
audio, “punchier” bass, and clearer highs, despite the iPad mini’s
significantly thinner design.
In practice, I think the new iPad mini sounds great. I’d choose
headphones or an external speaker for serious music or video
consumption, but day-to-day the iPad mini’s built-in speakers are
perfectly adequate. (I’d bet that this Acoustic Display technology
shows up in future iPhones too, and the iPad mini is serving as a
test bed of sorts.)
 ★

We opened a ticket with support about Gitbook availability issues and got this in reply. We have yet to see any official customer communication or breach notification. Apologies for the formatting, did the best I could as it's a mobile paste.
Update:
GitBook security incident update
 Hey ,
 The GitBook app, the GitBook API, and published docs are available again. A few services may still be degraded as we finish restoring everything to full performance.
*What happened*
 GitBook has been the target of a sophisticated, highly targeted attack using AI agents. 
 At 19:00 CET, November 2, the attacker gained unauthorized access to some of our infrastructure credentials. We detected the attack immediately and acted swiftly to block further impact. 
 To make sure our infrastructure was fully secure, we then took the GitBook app and authenticated docs sites offline. We kept publicly published content live for as long as possible, using cached data.
*What we did immediately*
* Blocked the attacker and closed the vulnerabilities involved
* Replaced every credential and secret across our infrastructure
* Brought services back only once we were confident they were secure
* Invalidated every customer’s API tokens on our platform
*Your data*
 Our investigation shows that the attacker may have accessed the following:
* Git Sync secrets.
* GitBook API tokens.
* Third-party API tokens used to connect external tools to GitBook.
* Questions asked to GitBook Assistant by your site visitors.
At this stage, we have found no evidence that any of your content in GitBook was modified.
*What you need to do now*
* Rotate any existing GitBook API tokens. We revoked all personal API tokens during the incident.
* Rotate any third-party API tokens or secrets you use to connect other tools to GitBook.
* If you have published integrations that use secrets, rotate those secrets.
* If you use the GitBook MCP server, re-authenticate it.
 Please contact your GitBook organization’s admin to assist with this process.
*What we are doing next*
* Monitoring the situation in case of further attacks.
* Introducing further security measures to our platform.
* Writing a full post mortem that will be published soon with more detailed information about the incident.
* If you have any further questions, please reach out to your account manager or our support team. You can also check status.gitbook.com for updates
Thank you for your patience, and we apologize again for the disruption
 The GitBook team

articles.title: Apple’s New iPhone Release Schedule Seems to Pay Off
articles.summary:
Horace Dediu, tweeting yesterday on Apple’s results:
iPhone grew at 17% sales which is amazing considering they did not
launch the 18 or the Duo or the new Air in the quarter.
The Duo didn’t launch until October, which is Q1 (in Apple’s financial calendar). And the Air, last year, was not a big seller (putting it lightly). The big bet Apple made this year was postponing the regular iPhone 18 until the end of winter early next year. The pro models — Pro and Pro Max — combined sell more than the regular non-pro no-adjective iPhone each year, but the regular non-pro iPhone is Apple’s single best-selling iPhone model. The bet that Apple made is that those mainstream buyers don’t care if the regular iPhone 18 ships five or six months after the 18 Pros — and won’t care next year, or the year after that, or the year after that about this same schedule being followed by the iPhones 19, 20, 21, etc.
The other factor at play is that the just-reported quarter started in July, just after Apple raised prices on just about every major product it sells other than the iPhone. So it’s theoretically possible that this quarter’s sales were boosted by people buying year-old iPhone 17-generation models in anticipation of Apple raising prices with the new models in September (which is exactly what happened). But I don’t see how that can explain 17 percent growth in sales year-over-year. Some savvy enthusiasts definitely did this. I have heard from a few people who bought iPhone 17 Pros in August, concluding that they’d be better off saving money than spending more for an only incrementally better 18 Pro (which would no longer come in the all-time-great cosmic orange colorway). But general consumers don’t follow Apple that closely. There are around 1.6 billion iPhone users worldwide, and I bet at least an entire billion of them have no idea that Apple always holds an iPhone introduction event in early September.
We can’t call this new launch schedule a win until we see what happens in late February or early March when Apple launches the iPhone 18, 18e, and Air 2, but so far it sure looks like a win.
 ★

articles.title: Steve Jobs on His Final Quarterly Analyst Call: ‘We Think the Open Versus Closed Argument Is Just a Smokescreen’
articles.summary:
After linking to it earlier today, I re-read Steve Jobs’s remarks from his last appearance on a quarterly analyst call. It’s a banger of a good read:
You know, even if Google were right, and the real issue is
“closed” versus “open,” it is worthwhile to remember that open
systems don’t always win. Take Microsoft’s “Plays For Sure” music
strategy, which used the PC model — which Android uses as well — of separating the software components from the hardware
components. Even Microsoft finally abandoned this “open” strategy
in favor of copying Apple’s integrated approach with their Zune
player, unfortunately leaving their OEMs empty-handed in the
process. Google flirted with this integrated approach with their
Nexus One phone.
In reality, we think the open versus closed argument is just a
smokescreen to try and hide the real issue, which is, “What’s best
for the customer — fragmented versus integrated?” We think
Android is very, very fragmented, and becoming more fragmented by
the day. And as you know, Apple strives for the integrated model
so that the user isn’t forced to be the systems integrator. We see
tremendous value at having Apple, rather than our users, be the
systems integrator. We think this a huge strength of our approach
compared to Google’s: when selling the users who want their
devices to just work, we believe that integrated will trump
fragmented every time.
Prescient.

articles.title: Prove you are not a child
articles.summary:
I'm 100% for banning social media for children. I would even extend it to banning it all together in its current form. But I am also against the methods for enforcement.
			
The problem with banning social media for one group and not another is that you have to differentiate the different groups somehow. And right now, in an age where information and personal data means everything, there are several entities that are salivating to get this data.
I've written before about all the problems that come from uploading sensitive data online. It doesn't even matter if they delete the data afterward, as long as the data goes through the wire in the first place, there is a chance for a leak.
What appears to be the same simple request "please verify your identity", becomes fundamentally different when mediated by technology. The question isn't whether these digital systems will be compromised, but when. And unlike that movie theater clerk who can't perfectly recall my birthdate minutes after seeing it, computers have perfect memory. They store, copy, backup, and transmit our most sensitive information through networks we don't control, to companies we've never heard of, under policies we'll never read.
When kids are not allowed to use social media, it's the adult who pays the price. It's the adult who has to prove that they are not children. They have to risk uploading their government ID to a third party, or biometric data that may be saved and backed up forever. 
I reject this method. 
I also reject the method where I have to provide my age to the operating system. No system should compel me to provide personal data in order to use it. Especially if this feature is intended to provide the information to a third party. And what happens if I don't provide this information to my freebsd machine? Or worse, what if I provide false information? Am I going to get punished? How does that protect children in any way?
Breaking news: Grown up arrested when OS reported forged identity in his laptop.
One question I asked myself was what happens when a minor circumvents the ban. What are the consequences? At least in Australia, a country that has implemented a social media ban for those under 16, there are no consequences.
The law places legal responsibility on platforms, not children or parents, and it currently applies to Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube.
This almost sounds reasonable. Why should you care, if it becomes facebook responsibility when you don't even own a facebook account? But there is always a caveat. When facebook becomes a tool your school uses to communicate with parents. When Google classroom is the service students use to do their homework. When you are required to login on a system to receive government service. You may not care about a particular social media, but they raise the bar for every other entrant in the game. Every website frequented by a large number of people inherently become social media, and demand data you didn't need to provide before.
Technology is not a magical thing that can just solve every problem. It is especially weak when it comes to social problems. However, society can use technology to solve their problems. The responsibility of children falls onto their parents. And there are great tools for parents that their kids access on their devices.

articles.title: Apple’s Analyst Calls Have Been Scripted for Decades
articles.summary:
Bloomberg opinion columnist Dave Lee:
Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the
philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday
were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings
call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a
carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.
This is stupid. I mean, it would have been fun if Ternus’s style on the analyst conference call had been loose and freewheeling. Just like it would have been fun if the questions from analysts hadn’t been mostly insipid and pointless. But nothing has changed here other than who the CEO is. Tim Cook’s quarter calls were snoozefests. Save those recordings and use them to help you sleep. And that’s exactly how Cook wanted them.
What Ternus should do is follow Steve Jobs’s lead, and skip these calls except when there’s something exceptional to address. Let CFO Kevan Parekh and COO Sabih Khan handle them, the way Jobs used to let Tim Cook and Apple’s then CFOs handle them. At one point in 2008, Jobs had only appeared on three of the calls in 11 years. He then appeared on the call in October 2008 to address the global financial crisis, and again in October 2010 (one year before he died) to celebrate Apple’s first $20 billion quarter and to throw shade at Android, BlackBerry, and competing tablets. In the 14 years of Jobs’s 2.0 stint as CEO, he only appeared on five quarterly calls. That’s the way to do it. Show up only when you have something worth saying. Otherwise the message remains clear: steady as she goes.
 ★

articles.title: Pluralistic: Separable (03 Nov 2026)
articles.summary: Today's links Separable: AI makes us deal with paintings without painters, words without writers and mathematics without mathematicians. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Haircase; There's no copyright policy; Sole and despotic dominion; Trump x fraud; Brexit requires an act of Parliament; Official Air Travel Replacement Knives; UK hospitals v malware. Upcoming appearances: Kilkenny, Courtenay, Vancouver, Folkestone, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Separable (permalink) Long before the Turing Test, there was the touring Edison Test: from 1915 to 1925, the scoundrel Thomas Edison put on a traveling show for his phonograph machine, touring venues around the USA. Edison set live performers and an Edison phonograph playing behind closed curtains that would be periodically pulled aside to reveal that the music the audience had taken to be live performance was actually a record player: https://www.tomedison.org/blog/edisons-tone-tests Now, if you've ever heard an Edison phonograph, this might seem like yet another tale in which old-timey people are revealed to be credulous yokels. You would never mistake one of those scratchy, hissing recordings for a live performance: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=96gIIFmEjY4 And indeed you wouldn't, but not because the phonograph predates the evolution of the human brain's anti-credulity lobe. The reason old-timey people couldn't tell the difference between a phonograph and a live performance was that before the phonograph, every live performance had a performer. The two were inseparable, and so when you encountered the sound of a musical performance, your brain would insist that there must be a performer as well. This is a well-understood principle in swindles, magic tricks and literature. It's the basis of Douglas Adams' towel gambit: For some reason, if a strag discovers that a hitchhiker has his towel with him, he will automatically assume that he is also in possession of a toothbrush, washcloth, soap, tin of biscuits, flask, compass, map, ball of string, gnat spray, wet-weather gear, space suit etc, etc. Furthermore, the strag will then happily lend the hitchhiker any of these or a dozen other items that the hitchhiker might accidentally have "lost." All persons heretofore encountered in possession of a towel had all that other stuff, so the mere presence of a towel evokes an overwhelming intuition that all that other stuff must be nearby. Like every conjuring trick and every swindle, this cognitive illusion swiftly regresses to the mean. After a few exposures to phonographs, the manifest differences between live performance and recordings become impossible to miss, and you stop making that mistake. If one thing always signifies the presence of another – if a towel always implies a backpack full of supplies or if a performance always implies a performer – there's no reason for you to entrain the neurological patterns needed to detect the performance without the performer. This doesn't mean that it's hard to develop the capacity to make this distinction, just that the ability to detect a phenomenon always post-dates your encounter with that phenomenon. You've no doubt guessed by now that this is an analogy about AI. The implication of this ability to learn to discern differences after you encounter them (but not before) implies that a chatbot might pass the Turing Test at its introduction, but then come to fail the test after we've all had the experience with it that lets us tune our perceptions to spot the differences, which then become as unmissable as the needle hiss on a phonographic reproduction of a concert pianist. This is an experience many of us have already had. Prior to chatbot-generated prose, we'd never had experience with writing that didn't have a writer. Prior to image-gen output, we'd never had experience with paintings that didn't have painters. At first, the output from these models was remarkable, and often indistinguishable from human-generated words and images. Even knowing that these works were extruded by an algorithm, it was hard to shake the conviction that they were the product of human creativity. These works were "eerie," in the sense that Mark Fisher uses, "the seeming of intent without an intender": https://pluralistic.net/2024/05/13/spooky-action-at-a-close-up/#invisible-hand Just like the strag inferring the existence of "toothbrush, washcloth, soap, tin of biscuits, flask, compass, map, ball of string, gnat spray, wet-weather gear, space suit etc, etc," we automatically imputed to these works both a creator and a creative impulse. We supposed that their words and brushstrokes represented aesthetic and technical choices emanating from human creators who meant something by them (or at least were so satisfied by the accident of their appearance on the page that they left them stand). These creators were figments of our imagination. No one is home inside the AI. The intentionality we imputed to these works was the actual "AI hallucination": https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/21/sunsetting/#oh-mr-sun-sun-mr-golden-sun-please-shine-down-on-me Just as important as the emergence of these hallucinations is their disappearance. For many of us, chatbots that used to pass the Turing Test now flunk it. The chatbots haven't gotten worse at impersonating humans, we've just gotten better at spotting the difference between a human and a bot, just as we got better at hearing the difference between a phonograph and a pianist. Writing without a writer and paintings without a painter are new phenomena, and learning to separate the formerly inseparable is the first step in our societal metabolization of these novelties. Recordings of musical performance have a place in our world, and so do performers. This separation process is currently underway in many disciplines, thanks to the extraordinary capital available to AI companies. These companies are incinerating that capital in a series of extremely flash demos that are intended to ensure that the supply of bales of $100 bills that they feed to their money furnaces ("data centers") never stops. Lately, AI companies have made headlines with a series of mathematical accomplishments that left mathematicians in an uproar and non-mathematicians in a muddle. Obviously, while mathematicians are qualified to assess these accomplishments, the rest of us are not. Beyond simple arithmetic, most of us don't do a lot of math on a regular basis, and even those of us who have to deploy a little geometry or stats typically don't engage with math at a theoretical level. To make things worse, math – like physics – is a crank-magnet. These highly abstract, closed systems rely on introspection to advance the field, and some of those advances have been contributed by untrained laity, so it can be hard to know if your amazing idea about physics or mathematics represents an outsider's breakthrough or an amateurish cul-de-sac. Every mathematician and physicist I know receives a steady stream of breathless, over-the-transom "proofs" that solve some long-standing problem in the field, and none of these experts in my orbit has ever found a breakthrough in this material. It's a rare expert who will even respond to these unsolicited manuscripts. That's not their job. As Teresa Nielsen Hayden says, "You are not responsible for the things you do in other people's dreams." Unfortunately, this is a situation that is perfectly suited to AI. If you've introspected your way into a mathematical "breakthrough" that no mathematician will discuss with you, you can avail yourself of any number of chatbots who will assure you that you've broken exciting new theoretical ground, and these chatbots will even act as "research collaborators," contributing more slop-physics or slop-math to your conclusions. Again, as far as I know, no one has actually made a breakthrough this way, and the major impact on the field from giving chatbots to excitable outsiders has been to make the unsolicited manuscripts much longer, with the veneer of professionalism that means an expert might have to give them a second or even third glance to realize that they're nonsense. But some working mathematicians have found chatbots to be extremely useful "collaborators." The most prominent of these is Terrence Tao, a Macarthur-winning mathematician who has excited many mathematicians and lay-people alike by publishing his chat-logs and the resulting mathematical work: https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/28/hitl-ers/#ai-ai-oh One way to understand Tao is as a "centaur," the automation theory term for a worker who is assisted by a machine. For all that Tao describes Chatgpt as his collaborator, it's clear from reading the chat-logs that it's Tao who drives the research agenda. He sets the questions and the direction of the answers. Chatgpt doesn't give him orders – it's the other way around. But for every problem Tao and Chatgpt solve together there are several mathematical problems that are being solved by chatbots without that kind of human collaboration. In particular, Openai has released a tsunami of "solutions" to longstanding mathematical problems, including some that carry large cash bounties and others that were posed by legends of the field, like Erdos. This is mathematics without a mathematician, and – as with all the other separations cleft by the AI companies – it's proving difficult to metabolize. Back in September, Fenner Stanley Tanswell published an opinion piece for the Mathematical Intelligencer entitled "The Enshittification of Mathematics" that tried to do just that: https://rdcu.be/5uYGc2uo454a Tanswell distinguishes between mathematics as a discipline practiced by mathematicians and the proofs and theorems that those mathematicians produce. He makes the point that when a mathematician finds the answer to some longstanding mathematical puzzle, they do so by creating "scaffolding" that bridges the new insight with the existing commons of mathematical understanding. The thing that makes a "solution" so exciting isn't that a problem has been solved – it's that the method for solving that problem prompts a cascading reconsideration of many other areas of mathematics, prompting shifts to large areas of the discipline. This point is made even more forcefully by Giordano Scarciotti, a complex systems researcher at Imperial College London and science communicator who vlogs under the Youtube handle "Prof Gio." Scarciotti's most successful video to date is "You Truly Don't Understand What Just Happened to Mathematics," published last month: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KqiDqJMxg6o "You Truly Don't Understand…" makes a similar point to Tanswell's, using a thought experiment in which we wake up one day and discover an American flag on the surface of Mars. Without knowing how that flag got to Mars, the mere fact of its existence doesn't help us get any closer to an actual Mars mission. The output of mathematical models is a series of faits accomplis, often accomplished through brute-force, or sometimes through opaque methods that lack the "scaffolding" that bridges these outcomes into the broader field of mathematics. Scarciotti cites Euler's work on the longstanding "Seven Bridges of Königsberg" problem, which asked whether it was possible to go on a walking tour of Königsberg such that you crossed each of the city's seven bridges only once: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Bridges_of_K%C3%B6nigsberg The point of that problem (and Euler's solution to it) wasn't to produce a set of Mapquest directions for a walking tour of Königsberg. In solving the Seven Bridges problem, Euler invented graph theory, an important area of mathematics that is routinely used today for many important applications, including computer networking. You can thank graph theory for helping to route the packets that brought these very words to you. So far, we've figured out how to get a model to either rule out the possibility of taking that each-bridge-only-once walk or to give us the route map. What this computer-generated "mathematics" is not doing is advancing the field. Tanswell points out that a world in which chatbots "solve" these problems is one where the role of mathematicians is reduced to being reverse centaurs, assistants to the machine whose job is to clean up after the chatbot's research agenda. But there's nothing about knowing that there's no route map for a seven-bridge walking tour that makes it easier to invent graph theory, and a mathematician might spend years working on the computer's "answer" to that problem only to conclude that the computer's solution didn't add any theoretical insight to the field. In other words, in a world where mathematicians and mathematics are inseparable, every solution to a longstanding problem heralds an accompanying theoretical insight. Once we separate mathematics from mathematicians, we start to get solutions without insights. These are a lot less interesting than the kinds of solutions that mathematicians come up with. This is a distinction the AI companies really don't want us to dwell on. We're meant to marvel at these very expensively derived solutions and conclude that the AI companies can be forgiven for spending $1T this year, even if they only grossed $50B in return. But (as Scarciotti notes), there are real-world consequences in our failure to grasp this distinction: if we convince early-career mathematicians and promising mathematics students that the world no longer needs mathematicians because "the AI can do their jobs," then we will choke off the supply of future mathematicians who we'll either need to work in a Terrence Tao-like, centaurish relationship with chatbots (good), or even to serve as reverse centaurs, marking the chatbots' homework to see if there are any theoretical insights to be found in it (bad). This is one of the underappreciated consequences of AI mania. AI bosses are particularly interested in convincing us that AI can do the job of skilled professionals in fields where there is a chronic undersupply of experts, like radiology. A chatbot that helps a (centaur) radiologist by suggesting that they double-check some of their results might indeed save lives. But a chatbot that produces thousands of radiology reports for a single (reverse centaur) radiologist to approve at a velocity that precludes careful scrutiny is going to kill people. Centaur radiology requires more radiologists, not fewer. A centaur radiologist processes fewer X-rays (because sometimes the chatbot tells them to double-check a diagnosis) than an unassisted radiologist. LLM-assisted radiology improves quality, not quantity. That's not what AI companies are selling. An AI company can't turn a profit by raising the cost of radiology (even if that improves the quality of radiological analyses). So the firehose of announcements from AI companies is always about putting radiologists out on the breadline – not about needing more radiologists, who will get a new radiology tool that helps them work better, if a little more slowly. The pronouncements of AI companies aren't just marketing hype, they're attempts at self-fulfilling prophecy. If you convince all the would-be radiologists that the profession is about to be vaporized by chatbots, those people will not study radiology, and then we will need to retask the dwindling supply of human radiologists to marking the chatbots' homework and hoping that they don't kill too many people by missing the chatbots' mistakes. That's the catastrophic outcome that both Scarciotti and Tanswell warn us of: if we convince people that we're heading into a world of mathematics without mathematicians, that's exactly what we'll get, because no one will try to become a mathematician. But because mathematics without mathematicians is a set of guide maps for crossing Königsberg's bridges (but not graph theory), then mathematics without mathematicians is also mathematics without mathematics. articles.title: Pumpkin Seeds
articles.summary:
Some spare ephemera about Halloween, at exactly the time you need it: A couple days after the fact. We got cryptids, celebs, and even an original tune.

Hey all, Ernie here with a piece from David Buck! He’s here to talk about the most tedious holiday, depending on how you hold it: Halloween. (It’s so tedious that we wrote about it late.)
Today in Tedium: Hey, everyone! I’m back! Anyhow, my love of Halloween isn’t dead, but it sure does smell funny these days. Over the past few years, we’ve published a few Halloween specials featuring plenty of spooky, Halloween-themed stuff. We even tried out a short video/podcast thingy. Last year, we presented a sequel of sorts. And this year, we’re continuing that tradition with some more Halloween-flavored treats for the spooky season. So grab yourself a Butterfinger, put on your favorite spooky tunes, and get ready for another helping of Pumpkin Spice Pop Culture. — David @ Tedium
Today’s GIF comes from a piece of classic cheese involving the late Tim Curry, one of the best to ever do it. More about that below.


1966

The year reports of a flying, humanoid monster being seen around Point Pleasant, WV. Sightings continued until late 1967. It was probably just migrating birds, but Mothman continued to be part of the public imagination. It’s perhaps just as recognizable as the Jersey Devil, Bigfoot, or Chupacabra in the Great Hall of Cryptids (an imaginary place I just made up, but, hey, it’d be a pretty bitchin’ museum).

(David Buck)
Cryptids are the cream of the Halloween crop
Halloween isn’t complete without monsters. I’ve read about them, played TTRPG’s that feature them, and even drawn a few, like that mushroom bit baba yaga-style house above.
A few years ago, I was an avid viewer of Dr. Emily Zarka’s Monstrum. It’s a show about the monsters of cultures all around the world. She’s covered by the headless horseman (so have we!), King Kong, and cryptids from around the world.
Monsters are always a fascinating topic, particularly lycanthropes. But we got to thinking more about local cryptids. That is, cryptids specific to a certain area. You know, like the Jersey Devil. Only they’re not limited to the United States. These cryptids and stories about them have traveled across the world.
Cryptids have long been a fascinating subject for us, so we did a little roundup of the four of the most interesting local cryptids we came across.
My criteria for these was a) I think they’re interesting and b) I can draw them. You’ll see why that’s important in a moment.
If your favorite cryptid isn’t here, I apologize. They’re all great. These just happen to be the ones I like the most right now.

Grafton Monster: Grafton, WV. Ah, West Virginia, home to the original sightings of Mothman. The state has another cryptid in its history: the Grafton Monster. It’s supposed to be a tall and pale humanoid creature that may or may not be headless. Oh, and it makes a creepy (sometimes described as “unusual” whistle sound.
Just like our good buddy Mothman up there, sightings of the Grafton Monster began around 1964. Journalist Robert Cockrell described the monster as roughly 7 to 9 feet tall. He also said it looked kind of like a seal but it had no head. I imagine it looks a little something like my drawing above (it’s not to scale).

Dover Demon: Dover, MA. The east coast seems to be awash in cryptids. Massachusetts has the Dover Demon. This one is pretty odd. In 1977, a creature with glowing orange eyes that was only four feet tall was spotted on a broken stone wall. 17-year old Bill Bartlett drew a sketch
Over the next few nights, more sightings were reported. What the kids described sounded like a gray alien right out of Area 51.
What they might have actually seen was a baby moose or a snow owl. Either way, it’s a bizarre local cryptid story and has become legendary around that area of Massachusetts.

Tommyknocker: Georgetown, Colorado. Did you know that Tommyknockers are a real Colorado cryptid? No, these aren’t Stephen King’s Tommyknockers. Instead, these guys are like Colorado leprechauns.
They knock on things from inside a mine. You can’t see them, but they’re there, warning of impending cave-ins or helping miners out.
Sometimes, they’re friendly or described as tricksters. But they’re a Colorado legend, right along with the Yeti’s in Vail, those pesky vampires in Lafayette, and that silly little hotel that inspired The Shining in Estes Park.

Bunyip: Australia. The U.S. has its fair share of local cryptids, but you should see some of the ones from around the world. Take the bunyip, for example. This thing is scary. It’s from aboriginal culture, originally, and is said to resemble a hippo. Or a manatee. Or something with an elongated neck.
Either way, it’s an incredibly deadly creature lurking in a swamp in the inner part of the continent. According to the Encyclopedia Britannica, its origin might be related to the rare appearances of seals upstream in Australia. I suppose that makes sense, but imagine running into one of these things in the wild.
Cryptids often seem to be based on things that really do exist, but the way we imagine or interact with them is what creates the idea of a monster. The human imagination really is a powerful thing, isn’t it?


2012

The year I wrote a silly song for Halloween. Back in those days, I wrote silly bluesy folk songs. I still do. But I used to do it a lot more often. And I had a ton of fun songs. I’ve never managed to get enough energy together to make a full record. Life has been hectic. Lately, I’ve decided I want to return to what I liked most about this industry: playing music and writing about oddball stuff. With that in mind, I wanted to share the journey of a Halloween-adjacent song I wrote over a decade ago and never got around to until now. So I dug this song up from its grave.

(Raisa Milova/Unsplash)
A brand-new, oddball song for Halloween that never got the chance to live
Last year, we talked about Phish’s famous Halloween shows and a lot of other Halloween-themed music from some of our favorite musicians. This year, my costume is “nerdy guy who’s really into jam bands.” When you look at me, you can just tell I like Blues Traveler. A lot. (Editor’s note: I also enjoy Blues Traveler … when John Popper is not blocking me on social media.) So, of course, I’ll be talking more about my own foray into “scary melodies”.
I’ve been reflecting on something related to my personal musical journey. About a decade ago (perhaps a few years earlier), I wrote what I considered a “Halloween song.” My goal was to make a video for it, release it online, and submit it to The Dr. Demento Show.
As I’ve written previously, getting airplay on Dr. Demento was a singular dream of mine for a long time. It did eventually happen, but not until a few years before Dr. D announced his retirement. It’s been a year since the show ended.
So where does that leave my career ambitions? I dunno. I’ve been honing my craft and playing for fun for years. So it doesn’t really affect things much. The weird music pipeline is just a bit different.
But I want to talk about that Halloween song I wrote so many years ago. I called it “Beware, the Poltergeist” because I thought it sounded fun and kind of cool. It might have been based on a short story or TV episode, but I just don’t exactly recall where it came from.
I started the song, wrote some music, and finished a verse/pre-chorus, but have just never been able to finish or expand it meaningfully. It’s a bluesy tune about a poltergeist who’s kind of a jerk. I thought it was hilarious, and I dig the way I have the melody match the lyric.
The song starts like this (it was originally in the key of B):
There’s a ghost in my house
Trying to push me down a staircase
There’s a ghost in my house
Throwing things all over the place
See? This is just proof that you don’t need an LLM to write a dumb song. I was writing dumb songs years before ChatGPT hit the scene. Also, don’t use an LLM to help you be creative. If you didn’t bother to write it yourself, I don’t want to read or listen to it. Hey, look! Some clouds. I’ll be right back.
(Incomprehensible ranting and light swearing about outsourcing thinking and creativity in the direction of no one in particular)
Okay. I’m back. Anyhow, I wrote a chorus/pre-chorus. It isn’t Vonnegut, but I like it. I’m not sure if I actually want it to say much. After that, the song repeats the “there’s a ghost in my house” bit, followed by an off-hand comment about how much he sucks.
Obviously, the song isn’t going to make it onto the show now. But that’s not the reason I revisit it every so often. I like it. It’s fun to play. I just never managed to finish it. The other day, however, I realized something: it actually is finished, and it always has been. I was just overthinking it and playing it in the wrong tuning.
Not everything needs to be edited or rewritten to death. Sometimes, there’s value in a simple song with an extended guitar bit.

I never recorded it. Until now. So, this Halloween, I present the second-ever released song by my one-man band (which I’m calling Asthmatic Whales nowadays; it used to be The Nostalgia Ward): “Beware, the Poltergeist.”
And there you have it. A silly Halloween song for the truly scary times we’re living in. I hope you enjoyed it as much as I did dusting it off and revisiting it. Thanks for reading, and I hope you have a very Happy Halloween.


Haunted Halloween ’86 may be one of the few homebrew games to appear in a big-name retail store.
Those homebrew NES games Spirit Halloween sells? Surprisingly good
In last year’s NES roundup, I briefly mentioned how Spirit Halloween was selling NES carts containing the homebrew title Haunted: Halloween ‘86: The Curse of Possum Hollow. What I didn’t talk about is just how freaking amazing this game series is.
Haunted: Halloween ‘85, and Haunted: Halloween‘87: Year of the Witch.
You can pick the games up on Steam or Itch.Io, from the folks who made it, Retrotainment Games LLC. All their stuff is great. There are also physical cartridges on their official website, if you’re into that sort of thing.
Haunted: Halloween ’85, as played on a 3DS. You don’t need an NES to enjoy this homebrew series, though it possibly helps.
These games are standouts among NES homebrew titles; they have a Double Dragon and Mighty Final Fight feel to them. However, the stories are more developed, you can switch characters, there are extra move sets (which is not typical in most NES games), and I had a ton of fun playing through them.
So let’s look at the trilogy. I only own the first two games (purchased directly from Itch.Io)
I haven’t had the opportunity to play Haunted: Halloween ‘87 yet, but if it’s anything like the first two (and particularly, like ‘86), I know I’m going to love it.
I think the first two are definitely standout titles and I recommend them for some 8-bit Halloween fun.
As far as NES Homebrew goes, I’m still pretty enthusiastic about it, all these years later.


33

The number of times I’ve mentioned or outright talked about The Dr. Demento show on Tedium. Although he’s been officially retired for a year now, I still listen to and collect the show. I haven’t been able to keep up with the community much (although I’d like to) due to life, but I know the fans are still out there. Halloween is a time we “Dementians” loved, so I always think about the show a lot more often around this time of year. I also couldn’t help but think that the good Doctor would have done a nice tribute to the late Tim Curry on his show back in August, if it hadn’t gone off the air.

This year has been a rough one, both for the world and in terms of some of our favorite entertainers passing.
We lost Tim Curry, Dolly Parton, and Patrick Stewart all within a few months of each other. In honor of these icons, here are a few fun facts about each that relate to Halloween:

Tim Curry once recorded a classic cheeseball song for the low-budget ’80s HBO movie The Worst Witch called “Halloween Song.” As Gizmodo wrote about it in 2020, “It has remained one of the most wonderful, terrible, bizarre videos of all time, thanks to its unapologetic synthesizer score, baffling lyrics, and the cheapest special effects the ‘80s had to offer—but there’s more to it than its cheesiness. Much more.” (Speaking of Curry, check out this Rocky Horror Picture Show audience participation recording from 1983.)
Dolly Parton was a Halloween enthusiast, and shared half a dozen separate costumes on her Instagram page last year. In the wake of her passing, her fans made her one of the most popular costume options this year.
Patrick Stewart reportedly bought a haunted house in Hollywood, then rented it to someone without telling his tenants about it. (They figured it out, and then he came clean.) It’s a tale that he wrote about in his book Making It So: A Memoir.

It’s a sad time, but hopefully, we’ve been able to cheer you up and boost your spirits a bit during this Halloween season (which seems to be shrinking each year, or maybe I’m just getting old). Thanks for reading, and until next time, have a very Happy Halloween!
